#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)
Description: The Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions is a quarterly panel survey that provides national summary data on the revenues, expenditures, and composition of assets of the largest defined benefit public employee pension systems for state and local governments. Data are collected on the financial holdings and activities of the largest public-employee pension systems. The financial holdings data show assets in various types of securities such as stocks, bonds, federal notes, and mortgages. Revenue data consist of earnings, as well as contributions from governments and employees. Expenditure data consist primarily of payments to beneficiaries and withdrawals.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

messages.content:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)
Description: The Quarterly Summary of Public Pensions is a quarterly panel survey that provides national summary data on the revenues, expenditures, and composition of assets of the largest defined benefit public employee pension systems for state and local governments. Data are collected on the financial holdings and activities of the largest public-employee pension systems. The financial holdings data show assets in various types of securities such as stocks, bonds, federal notes, and mortgages. Revenue data consist of earnings, as well as contributions from governments and employees. Expenditure data consist primarily of payments to beneficiaries and withdrawals.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.

Let me get the govinfo PDF version.# Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP): research report

## Bottom line

Your title and description are essentially correct. A few details need fixing or qualifying:

1. **Name.** The official program name is the **Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)**. Your description says "Quarterly *Summary* of Public Pensions." That isn't your mistake: Census's own About page uses that wording, and the 2009 bridge report uses yet another name. Your description matches the Census About page almost word for word, including its typo ("withdrawls").
2. **Scope.** "The largest" systems means a fixed panel of the **100 largest** state and local defined benefit systems. It is not a sample of all public pensions.
3. **Old basis.** The panel is still drawn from the **2012 Census of Governments**. Census says it covers 87.2% of financial activity among these systems, but its FAQ page gives 87.5%.

## 1. Who publishes it

- **Publisher:** U.S. Census Bureau (Department of Commerce). The 2011 Federal Register notice named the Employment and Benefit Statistics Branch of the Governments Division as the responsible office. The time-series pages now list the contact as sssd.econ.data@census.gov.
- **Funding:** The FAQ says the survey "is part of the Recurring Programs Area and is funded with money appropriated by the U.S. Congress."

## 2. Legal authority and mandate

- **Statute:** Title 13 U.S.C. §§161 and 182. The About page and the F-10 form cite both sections. The FAQ and the 2011 Federal Register notice cite only §182. §161 covers the five-year Census of Governments, which supplies the panel. §182 authorizes surveys between censuses, which is what the quarterly collection is.
- **Paperwork Reduction Act clearance:** OMB control number **0607-0143**, form **F-10**. The most recent extension request I found was published June 6, 2024 (89 FR 48365), "without change." Census estimates 100 respondents, about 45 minutes each (30 minutes to 2 hours), 300 burden hours a year, and $0 cost to respondents. Earlier notices appeared in 2011 (76 FR 53402) and 2018.
- **Participation is voluntary.**
- **Not confidential:** The form says the data fall under 13 U.S.C. §9(b), which exempts information "customarily" kept in public records from Census's usual confidentiality rules.
- **Origin:** Census started the survey in **1968 at the request of the Council of Economic Advisers and the Federal Reserve Board**.

## 3. History

- **1968:** Quarterly collection begins.
- **Earlier names:**
  - "Finances of Selected Public Employee-Retirement Systems," a printed quarterly in the Governments Quarterly Report **GR series**. Its federal library classification number is **C 3.242**; the Free Library of Philadelphia holds issues from 1975 to 1994.
  - "Survey of the Finances of Public Employee Retirement Systems."
  - Renamed QSPP **effective Q1 2012**.
- **Panel size over time:**

  | Years | Systems in panel |
  |---|---|
  | 1969–73 | 100 |
  | 1974–76 | 111 |
  | 1977–79 | 106 |
  | 1980–82 | 105 |
  | 1983–84 | 102 |
  | 1985–94 | 104 |
  | 1995–99 | No panel information available |
  | 2000–present | 100 |

- **Panel redraws** (Census calls redrawing after each Census of Governments "best practice"):
  - **Q1 2009:** based on the 2007 Census of Governments; 5 systems replaced; covered 89.4% of activity. A bridge report was published (GOVSRR2009-3).
  - **Q1 2014:** based on the 2012 Census; covered 87.2%.
  - I found **no evidence of a redraw from the 2017 or 2022 Census of Governments.**
- **Classification changes:**
  - Q1 2012: realized and unrealized gains split apart; federal agency securities moved from corporate bonds to federal securities; private equity, venture capital and leveraged buyouts moved from "other securities" to corporate stocks.
  - Earlier: federal agency securities and mortgages were reclassified in 1987–89, the government contributions definition changed in Q4 2004, and investment earnings excluded imputed data from Q2 2002 to Q3 2004.
  - Q1 2010: the Denver Public Schools Retirement System merged into Colorado PERA, which inflated government contributions for that quarter.
- **Method change:** A new imputation approach started in Q2 2013. It groups similar systems and fills gaps using mean or median growth rates or direct substitution.

## 4. Content and methodology

- **Who is in it:** Defined benefit plans sponsored by state or local governments whose members are paid with public funds. Defined contribution plans and retiree health (OPEB) plans are excluded. Systems are ranked by total cash and security holdings in the latest Census of Governments.
- **What the form collects:**
  - **Revenues:** investment earnings, with realized and unrealized gains reported separately, plus government and employee contributions.
  - **Expenditures:** mainly benefit payments and withdrawals.
  - **Holdings:** stocks, bonds, federal securities, mortgages and other assets.
- **Timing:** Figures are as of the end of each calendar quarter. Due dates are about May 15, Aug 14, Nov 12 and Feb 11. Results come out about **three months after each quarter** as three summary tables covering the past five years.
- **Revisions:** Respondents can submit late data or revisions for up to 8 quarters, according to the FAQ. The 2024 notice says the previous seven quarters plus the current one. Revised figures are marked "R."
- **Response rates** (unit = number of systems responding out of 100; asset-weighted = share of assets those systems hold):

  | Quarter | Unit rate | Asset-weighted rate |
  |---|---|---|
  | 2024 (all quarters) | 96–99 | 97–99% |
  | Q2 2025 | 91 | 93.9% |
  | Q3 2025 | 83 | 90.0% |
  | Q4 2025 | 83 | 87.7% |
  | Q1 2026 | **76** | **82.1%** |

  The methodology page says at least 80% of systems give usable replies. The 2024 Federal Register notice says 70–80%. **The Q1 2026 rate is below the documented standard**, and the decline is worth watching.
- **Recent values:** Total cash and security holdings (FRED series QPRHLDTOTTOTHOLDINGSUSNO) were **$6.55 trillion in Q2 2026**, up from $6.12 trillion in Q1 2026 and $5.77 trillion in Q2 2025. Census reported $4.64 trillion for Q1 2021.

## 5. Caveats for analysts

- **It's a fixed panel, not a probability sample.** The 2009 bridge report says results "cannot be used to infer distributions for the entire universe" and cannot be weighted up to a national total.
- **There is no sampling error, but there is nonsampling error:** nonresponse, imputation, classification mistakes and reporting errors.
- **Accounting is mixed.** Some systems report on an accrual basis and some on a cash basis, so quarterly revenues minus expenditures won't match the change in holdings. Census says the differences usually resolve within the fiscal year.
- **Panel breaks** in 2009 and 2014, plus the classification changes above, interrupt the time series. Read the bridge reports and user notes before modeling long periods.
- **The panel's coverage share is out of date.** The 87.2% figure is based on 2012 rankings.
- **It measures assets, not liabilities.** QSPP says nothing about actuarial liabilities or funded ratios. For those, use the Federal Reserve's Financial Accounts table L.120.b or plan reports.
- **Rough cross-check (my own calculation, with different definitions):** QSPP holdings at end-2025 were $6.14 trillion. The Fed's figure for "defined benefit entitlements funded by assets," for all state and local plans, was $6.85 trillion. That ratio is about 90%, which fits the panel's coverage.

## 6. Users and uses

- **Federal Reserve Board:** The FAQ calls it the "primary user." The data feed the quarterly Financial Accounts of the United States (Z.1, formerly called Flow of Funds), state and local pension tables L.120 and L.120.b.
- **Bureau of Economic Analysis:** A primary source for the government sector of the national accounts (GDP/NIPA).
- **Others:** investment bankers and analysts tracking how these large institutional investors allocate assets, economists and public policy researchers using econometric models, journalists, and pension watchdog and advocacy groups.

## 7. Public benefit

- It is the **most timely official federal measure** of state and local pension finances. The annual survey and the five-year census lag far behind.
- It tracks trillions of dollars in assets that back the retirement income of public employees such as teachers and police, and that taxpayers ultimately support through government contributions.
- It shows quarter-to-quarter movements in contributions, benefit payments and investment mix, which matter for budget pressure and market analysis.
- The data are free and not confidential, and the series goes back to 1968.

## 8. Access points

- **Program page:** census.gov/programs-surveys/qspp. It has technical documentation, methodology, the F-10 questionnaire, user notes and the bridge report.
- **Current release:** census.gov/data/tables/time-series/econ/qspp/current-release.html. As of my research, the latest is **Q2 2026**, released around late September 2026. It includes tables, a **Unit ID file listing the 100 systems** (fixed-length text) and a file layout.
- **Time-series tool:** census.gov/econ/currentdata, program code **QPR**, with data from 1968 onward.
- **FRED** carries the series, and **ALFRED** keeps past vintages, which is useful because the data get revised.
- **API:** The documentation links to a "Public Sector: Annual and CoG API." I could not confirm that QSPP itself is served through it.

## 9. Preservation notes

- **Save each quarter's Unit ID file.** Panel membership changes with redraws and mergers, and only the current file is posted.
- **Save every release, not just the latest.** Revisions overwrite earlier numbers. ALFRED and the Wayback Machine hold some older versions.
- **Pre-digital volumes** (GR series, C 3.242) are in federal depository library collections. Census historical tables cover the earlier years, with footnotes.
- **Also archive:** the bridge reports (2009 report GOVSRR2009-3 and the 2012-based report), the questionnaire versions (the current F-10 is dated 05-05-2025), the methodology page, the user notes and the OMB supporting statements on reginfo.gov.

## 10. Related datasets

- Census **Annual Survey of Public Pensions** and the **Census of Governments: Survey of Public Pensions** (forms F-11 and F-12). These cover the full universe of about 6,000 systems at the plan level.
- Census Quarterly Summary of State & Local Tax Revenue.
- Federal Reserve Z.1 tables L.120, L.120.b and L.120.c.
- BEA national accounts (NIPA).
- **Public Plans Data**, plan-level data produced by the Center for Retirement Research at Boston College, MissionSquare Research Institute, NASRA and GFOA.

# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

I'll start by checking the ICR status, recent release timing, and Census Bureau staffing and budget news.The ICR is active until December 31, 2027. Next I'll check whether recent QSPP releases were delayed and whether anything QSPP-specific has changed.The ICR runs to the end of 2027, and the user notes page hasn't been updated since 2021. Next I'll check budget and reorganization proposals that might affect the government-finance surveys.The Government Units Survey (another public-sector survey) was discontinued in April 2025, and the annual pension form (F-11) is being streamlined. Now I'll try the staffing tracker.# Risk assessment: Quarterly Survey of Public Pensions (QSPP)

QSPP itself is in good shape today. Older data are still available, releases are coming out on time, and its Paperwork Reduction Act approval is current. The risks come from the agency around it: Census has lost staff and leadership, budgets are tightening, QSPP isn't required by law, and response rates are falling. I found no announcement that targets QSPP directly.

## 1. Historical Data Availability: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- Census's time-series tool (program code QPR) still serves quarterly data from 1968 to the present.
- FRED carries the series, and ALFRED keeps earlier versions of the numbers.
- The technical documentation is still posted, including the bridge reports, the F-10 form and the user notes.
- I found no evidence of removed files or changed historical values.

**Evidence pointing toward higher risk:**
- Only the current list of the 100 systems in the panel (the "Unit ID file") is posted. Older lists aren't archived on the site. This is long-standing practice, not a recent removal.
- Revisions overwrite earlier figures, so past versions survive only in ALFRED and the Wayback Machine.
- The user notes page hasn't been updated since October 2021.

**Why this level:** Nothing has been removed or altered. The gaps are archiving weaknesses, not losses.

## 2. Future Data Availability: **No Known Issue**

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- The approval to collect (OMB 0607-0143, ICR 202409-0607-003) is **active**. OMB approved it without change on 12/04/2024, and it expires **12/31/2027** ([omb.report](https://omb.report/icr/202409-0607-003)).
- The F-10 form was reissued 05-05-2025.
- The Q2 2026 release came out about September 17, 2026. That matches the usual schedule of roughly three months after each quarter.

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- The October 1 to November 12, 2025 government shutdown stopped collection and processing at Census ([Census Project](https://thecensusproject.org/2025/12/08/census-bureau-recovery-plan-for-economic-indicators-post-shutdown/)). Q3 2025 data were eventually published, but I couldn't confirm whether that release was delayed.
- The approval must be renewed again in 2027, under a reduced budget.

**Why this level:** Releases are on time and the approval is valid for more than a year.

## 3. Data Quality: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence for "Moderate Risk":**
- **Response is falling.** The share of the 100 systems responding was 96–99 in 2024. It fell to 91 in Q2 2025, 83 in Q3 and Q4 2025, and **76 in Q1 2026**. The asset-weighted rate fell from 97–99% to 82.1%.
- Q1 2026 is below the documented standard of at least 80% usable responses. Lower response means more imputed figures and bigger later revisions.
- **The panel is out of date.** It was last redrawn from the 2012 Census of Governments. Census calls redrawing after each census "best practice," but there was no redraw from the 2017 or 2022 censuses.
- **Related programs are shrinking:**
  - The Government Units Survey, which maintains the list of governments used to build these panels, was discontinued April 14, 2025 ([Census](https://www.census.gov/topics/public-sector/government-organization.html)).
  - An August 2026 Federal Register notice proposes combining items on the annual pension form (F-11) and **dropping 16 actuarial items** ([FR 2026-16791](https://www.federalregister.gov/documents/2026/08/18/2026-16791/agency-information-collection-activities-submission-to-the-office-of-management-and-budget-omb-for)). That is a sign of a broader streamlining push in public-sector statistics.

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- Detail, timing and frequency are unchanged: quarterly releases, the same three tables, the same panel of 100 systems.

**Why this level:** Nothing has been cut yet, but response rates and an aging panel are a real emerging threat to accuracy and timeliness.

## 4. Statutory Context: **Moderate Risk**

**Evidence for "No Known Issue":**
- The legal authority is named explicitly: 13 U.S.C. §§161 and 182, cited in the approval package.
- No other source gives quarterly, aggregate figures on public pension finances.
- The Federal Reserve is the primary user. Its Financial Accounts tables L.120 and L.120.b rely on the survey, and BEA uses it for the government sector of the national accounts.

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- §182 *permits* surveys between censuses ("may"). It doesn't require this one or say what it must collect.
- Participation is voluntary.
- Partial substitutes exist, though none is quarterly: the Annual Survey of Public Pensions, Public Plans Data, and plan financial reports.
- The FY2026 Census budget justification promises to eliminate "functions that are not statutorily mandated or core to the Bureau's mission" ([GovExec](https://www.govexec.com/workforce/2025/07/census-has-long-struggled-staffing-shortages-employees-say-trump-making-it-worse/406840/)). QSPP isn't statutorily mandated.

**Why this level:** It has named authority and important federal users, but no legal requirement, which leaves it open to discretionary cuts.

## 5. Staffing and Funding: **High Risk**

**Evidence for "High Risk":**
- **At least 1,300 Census employees left** through deferred resignation, early retirement and similar programs, according to AFGE ([AP](https://apnews.com/article/census-bureau-doge-federal-surveys-fe560e377be69e913660a6d90c1ee419)). The American Statistical Association estimates about a **15% staffing loss** since FY24 ([ASA](https://www.amstat.org/docs/default-source/amstat-documents/the-nations-data-at-risk-2025/census.pdf)).
- **Leadership has turned over:**
  - Director Santos resigned in early 2025.
  - Career acting director Ron Jarmin was replaced in September 2025 by George Cook, a political appointee who also serves as acting Under Secretary for Economic Affairs ([NPR](https://www.npr.org/2025/09/19/nx-s1-5288846/trump-census-bureau-director-george-cook)).
  - There were 18 vacancies among top leaders.
- **Current Surveys funding**, the account that funds QSPP, is shrinking:

  | Year | Amount | Change |
  |---|---|---|
